title: Equilibrium
full_review:
"Equilibrium" (Dimension) is set in a future where World War III has devastated Earth and any show of human emotion is punishable by death.

Watching this movie should have been an alternate choice since it is more punishment than reward. It borrows heavily from other sci-fi movies such as "Farenheit 451," "The Matrix," "THX 1138" and "Gattaca," yet its presentation is pretentious, as if it is breaking new ground in the genre.

Writer-director Kurt Wimmer's narrative is at times contradictory and the action scenes far from believable, but most of all his choice of Christian Bale to play the central character dooms the film. Bale gives a cold, empty performance with no depth and, although he is supposed to go through a tremendous transformation, he can't move us, even when he is weeping. His portrayal is similar to his vicious title role in "American Psycho."

Bale plays Preston, one of the top law enforcers, known as "Clerics" in post-nuclear Libria. The top Cleric, never seen, has decreed that feelings are what lead to war, so they are banned -- and everyone must self-inject drugs daily to keep them calm and obedient. Skipping medication is also a capital crime. Artifacts such as concealed books, recordings and paintings are instantly incinerated. (Who knew that the "Mona Lisa" would turn up in Libria only to be torched?)

Emotionless Preston apparently harbors no anger that his wife was executed four years earlier but when he kills his cleric partner (Sean Bean) for reading poetry he is disturbed, and secretly stops taking his equilibrium drugs. His ambitious new partner Brandt (Taye Diggs) watches him closely as they look for the active resistance movement in the Nethers zone. When they arrest the lovely Mary (Emily Watson, wasted in a brief role) Preston decides to support the rebels even as he promises his boss (Angus MacFayden) to infiltrate and crush the resistance.

One wonders about the anti-religious implications of naming the killer cops Clerics, calling their leader Father, and a speech by the second-in-command -- who equates obedience with faith. Preston is seen early on as a judge, jury and executioner with a stained-glass window behind him -- a cleric who can kill with impunity.

The action scenes grow increasingly violent as Preston is able to single-handedly take on up to a dozen armed men at a time and emerge intact. The deadly confrontations alternate between chop-socky bouts which look ridiculous and murderously extended shootouts.

An oppressive choral music track adds little to the mostly gray visuals. It's a clear case of cheap manipulation when the filmmaker stoops to using an endangered cute dog as a device to test Preston's resolve to change.

Even in these troubled times, the concluding revolution to restore freedom makes little emotional impact given the unconvincing narrative that precedes it.

Because of excessive violence and an instance of profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
